newsitem.title: SPAIN: Socialists decry Aznar ally's Bank of Spain seat.
newsitem.headline: Socialists decry Aznar ally's Bank of Spain seat.

text.p: Spain's opposition Socialists voiced outrage on Tuesday at a decision by the ruling conservative Popular Party (PP) to dispose of an unwanted deputy by seating him on the board of the central bank .

Luis Ramallo, a flamboyant and controversial member of parliament, was appointed on Monday as deputy head of Spain's markets watchdog -- a job which automatically makes him one of the Bank of Spain's non-executive directors.
"We feel it breaks with a tradition of respect (for central bank independence)," a Socialist spokeswoman told Reuters. "He's too political."
During nearly two decades as a member of parliament, Ramallo earned a reputation for long-winded, inflammatory attacks on opponents -- and more recently on friends.

One of the Socialists' more ardent critics when they were in power, he recently turned on the new PP government's independent defence minister, much to the embarrassment of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar.

Earlier this year, at a PP rally, Ramallo rambled on well past his allotted time despite Aznar's visible impatience and even the organisers' unsubtle playing of the party anthem through loudspeakers to drown him out.
He also drew criticism when he leaked sensitive details of the work of a parliamentary committee investigating illegal payments to Luis Roldan, disgraced former head of the paramilitary Civil Guard.
"Politically, there have been times when he hasn't exactly been discreet," the Socialist spokeswoman said.
Ramallo's appointment to the Bank of Spain board will not make him privy to monetary policy decisions, which are taken by a smaller committee.
But his departure from parliament was seen as conveying a conciliatory message to the government's allies.

Josep Oliver i Alonso, a professor at Barcelona University, said it indicated Aznar's party no longer needed political mavericks suited to the aggressive tactics of opposition and was aiming for more stable alliances with minority regional parties.
"It implies...the reinforcement of a tendency to strike pacts," he said.
Aznar, who took over in May after nearly 14 years of Socialist rule, needs the support of Catalonia's ruling coalition in order to make up a majority in parliament.
"In this context, there is no room for loud, critical voices (like Ramallo's)," said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America in Madrid.
